hooks.text: Commanded to shut down its systems to survive deep space.
Why would controllers command a healthy spacecraft to shut down?
Thirty-one months of radio silence ended with a three-word greeting.

title: The 31-Month Deep Space Alarm Clock
description: The solar-powered Rosetta probe survived thirty-one months of radio-silent hibernation before a pre-programmed alarm clock woke it up near a comet.

beats.text: Commanded to shut down its systems to survive deep space.
beats.visual: Artist illustration of the Rosetta spacecraft drifting in deep space, ESA, 2011.

beats.text: In 2004, the European Space Agency launched Rosetta on an [Ariane](/ˈɑɹˈiˈɑn/) 5 rocket.
beats.visual: Photograph of the Ariane 5 rocket launching Rosetta from Kourou, 2004.

beats.text: The probe gained speed through four planetary gravity assists around Earth and Mars.
beats.visual: Rosetta OSIRIS camera image of Mars during the planetary gravity assist flyby, 2007.

beats.text: It then completed flybys of two distant asteroids while pushing farther into the cold.
beats.visual: Rosetta OSIRIS camera photograph of asteroid 21 Lutetia during flyby, 2010.

beats.text: Nearly 800 million kilometers from the Sun, solar light was too weak to power its systems.
beats.visual: Diagram showing Rosetta solar panel arrays extended in deep space, ESA, 2004.

beats.text: Mission control initiated thirty-one months of radio-silent hibernation where only a clock remained active.
beats.visual: Mission controllers inside the European Space Operations Centre monitoring Rosetta hibernation, 2011.

beats.text: On January 20, 2014, that internal alarm clock triggered a wake-up signal received by NASA’s Goldstone station.
beats.visual: Photograph of the 70-meter Deep Space Network antenna at Goldstone receiving signal, 2014.
queries: Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex DSS-14

beats.text: Rosetta greeted Earth with 'Hello, world!' before becoming the first craft to orbit a comet.
beats.visual: OSIRIS image of Comet 67P double-lobed nucleus taken from Rosetta orbit, 2014.
